cls: Selective cannabinoid CB1 receptor antagonist/inverse agonist (anti-obesity agent - WITHDRAWN)
pharm: Selectively blocks the central and peripheral CB1 endocannabinoid receptor, reducing the overactivity of the endocannabinoid system that drives appetite and lipogenesis, thereby reducing food intake and improving metabolic parameters - but with significant psychiatric adverse effects.
quick: 20 mg once daily in the morning (as previously marketed; now withdrawn)
Was taken before breakfast, with or without food
Use with caution in severe renal impairment (not recommended)
Not recommended in severe hepatic impairment
Caution; depression/psychiatric risk may be worsened
Mood, depression, and suicidality - the reason for withdrawal
summary: Rimonabant was a selective CB1 cannabinoid receptor antagonist/inverse agonist developed for the treatment of obesity and overweight with associated risk factors, marketed in Europe (as Acomplia) from 2006. It reduced appetite and improved weight, waist circumference, lipids, and glycemic control. However, it markedly increased the risk of serious psychiatric adverse effects - depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation/behavior. Because of this risk it was suspended by the European Medicines Agency in 2008 and subsequently withdrawn worldwide; it was never approved by the US FDA. It is included here for reference only and should NOT be prescribed.
indications: (Historical / withdrawn) Adjunct to diet and exercise for obese patients (BMI >=30) or overweight patients (BMI >27) with associated risk factors such as type 2 diabetes or dyslipidemia

dosage.d: 20 mg once daily, taken in the morning before breakfast

admin: DO NOT PRESCRIBE - withdrawn from the market for psychiatric/suicide risk
(Historical) Was taken as a single 20 mg dose once daily in the morning
(Historical) Used with a mildly hypocaloric diet and increased physical activity
(Historical) Required screening and ongoing monitoring for depression and suicidality
(Historical) Treatment was to be stopped if depressive symptoms emerged
moa: Rimonabant is a selective antagonist (and inverse agonist) of the cannabinoid type 1 (CB1) receptor. The endocannabinoid system, acting through CB1 receptors in the central nervous system (notably hypothalamus and mesolimbic reward pathways) and in peripheral tissues (adipocytes, liver, gastrointestinal tract, skeletal muscle), is overactive in obesity and promotes appetite, food reward, lipogenesis, and insulin resistance. By blocking CB1 receptors, rimonabant reduces food intake and improves lipid and glucose metabolism and adiponectin levels. However, CB1 blockade in mood-regulating circuits also removes a tonic anxiolytic/antidepressant endocannabinoid influence, producing depression, anxiety, and suicidality - the adverse effects that led to its withdrawal.

absolute: Major depression and/or ongoing antidepressant treatment
Current or history of severe psychiatric illness
Known hypersensitivity to rimonabant or any component
relative: History of depression or suicidal ideation
Concurrent potent CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers
monitor: Emergence of suicidal ideation or behavior
Weight, waist circumference, and metabolic parameters

preg: There are insufficient data on use in pregnant women; animal studies are inconclusive but show potential developmental effects. Rimonabant was not recommended during pregnancy. (Product withdrawn.)
lact: Rimonabant is excreted in the milk of lactating animals and was contraindicated during breastfeeding. (Product withdrawn.)
renal: No specific dosage recommendation could be made for severe renal impairment, and use was not recommended in this group because of limited data. (Product withdrawn.)
hepatic: Rimonabant is metabolized by the liver (CYP3A4 and amidohydrolase). It was not recommended in severe hepatic impairment due to limited data; caution applied in moderate impairment. (Product withdrawn.)

major: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, clarithromycin, telithromycin, nefazodone) - increase rimonabant exposure
Antidepressants / contraindicated in patients on antidepressant therapy for major depression
moderate: CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, St. John's wort) - reduce rimonabant exposure
Other centrally acting agents that may worsen mood
minor: Possible additive effects with other weight-affecting drugs
interactions.food: Could be taken with or without food; a high-fat meal modestly increased exposure.
interactions.alcohol: Caution - alcohol may worsen the depressive/psychiatric adverse effects.

serious: Suicidal ideation and suicidal behavior (including completed suicide)
emergency: Acute severe depression or psychiatric crisis

monitoring: Mood and depressive symptoms at each visit (critical)
Suicidal ideation or behavior - discontinue immediately if present
counsel: This medicine has been withdrawn from the market and should not be used
(Historical) Stop the medicine and contact a doctor at once if you feel depressed, hopeless, or have thoughts of harming yourself
(Historical) Tell your doctor about any history of depression or mental illness before use
(Historical) It was meant to be used with a reduced-calorie diet and more activity
(Historical) Report new or worsening anxiety, mood changes, or sleep problems
Discuss safer, approved options for weight management with your clinician
pk: Appetite reduction over the first weeks of therapy
Long; approximately 6-9 days (longer in obese patients due to tissue distribution)
Once-daily dosing; prolonged due to long half-life
pearls: WITHDRAWN: EMA suspended Acomplia (rimonabant) in 2008 and it was withdrawn worldwide for serious psychiatric adverse effects (depression, suicidality); never FDA-approved - do NOT prescribe
Mechanistic lesson: CB1 receptor blockade reduces appetite but removes a protective endocannabinoid effect on mood
Contraindicated in major depression or in patients on antidepressants
Very long half-life (~6-9 days) means effects and risks persist after stopping
Source: EMA/SmPC and published trial data (RIO program) - not openFDA, as the drug was never US-approved
Serves as a key example in pharmacology of a target with on-target central toxicity
missed: Not applicable - this product has been withdrawn from the market and should not be used. (Historically: a missed once-daily dose was to be skipped if close to the next dose, without doubling up.)
overdose: There is limited human overdose experience. Management would be supportive and symptomatic, with particular attention to psychiatric status (depression, suicidality) and monitoring; there is no specific antidote. Given the long half-life, prolonged observation is appropriate.
